_comment: Transcribed by hand from selection-chart.pdf -- the 'HOW TO CHOOSE A WELDER' chart.
That file is one page, zero characters of text, one 1200x1200 JPEG. Every fact
below exists ONLY as pixels. Nothing here can be checked against page text the way
the other four tables are, so this table is marked textVerifiable:false and the
verifier enforces a different rule on it: any claim that CAN be corroborated in the
owner's manual must cite where, and the rest are shown to the user alongside a crop
of the chart itself so the picture is the citation.
This is the chart the brief calls out by name: 'some critical information exists
only in images (the welding process selection chart, ...)'.
thicknessNote: Gauge-to-inch conversions below are the standard US sheet-steel gauge and are OURS, not the chart's. The chart prints only the gauge label; the decimal is shown so a thickness can be range-checked, and is labelled as derived wherever it is displayed.

_comment: The chart is the third source that settles page 28's 'AC TIG Welding is used to
weld aluminum' line. The chart splits TIG in two: steel/stainless/chrome-moly are
marked 'DC TIG REQUIRED', aluminium and magnesium are marked 'AC TIG REQUIRED'.
Page 7 lists this machine's TIG materials as exactly the first group and its output
as DC. So page 28 is not describing a capability of this welder -- it is describing
what AC TIG is for, on a machine that does not have it.
acTigResolution.conclusion: This welder cannot TIG aluminium. Aluminium goes through the optional spool gun on MIG.

dutyCycleDefinition._comment: The chart also defines duty cycle in plain words and gives a worked example. The 165 A figure is the chart's generic illustration, NOT a rating for this machine -- this welder's own 30% point is 175 A. Kept here so nothing downstream mistakes it for a rated point.
dutyCycleDefinition.definition: The Duty Cycle is the number of minutes, within a 10 minute period, a welding process can produce the specified welding current without overheating.
